title: How to Make Spiralized Vegetable Skewers for a Healthy BBQ Side Dish
meta_description: Elevate your grill game with colorful spiralized vegetable skewers. Learn the best prep tips and recipes for a low-carb, healthy BBQ side dish.
html:
When most people think of BBQ side dishes, they picture heavy potato salads or corn on the cob. But if you're looking for something vibrant, low-carb, and visually stunning, spiralized vegetable skewers are the way to go. By twisting your veggies into curls rather than cutting them into chunks, you create more surface area for marinades to cling to and a unique texture that chars beautifully over an open flame.

The secret to getting those perfect, tight curls is using a quality Vegetable Spiralizer. Whether you prefer a handheld version for quick tasks or a countertop model for larger batches, a dedicated spiralizer turns dense root vegetables and soft squashes into elegant ribbons that wrap around a skewer like colorful springs.

Selecting the Best Veggies for Spiralized Vegetable Skewers

Not every vegetable handles the spiralizing-to-grilling pipeline the same way. You want a mix of structural integrity and moisture content. If a vegetable is too watery, it will collapse into a mushy mess on the grill; if it's too hard, it won't wrap around the skewer easily.

Zucchini and yellow squash are the gold standards here. They spiralize effortlessly and soften just enough to hold their shape. Carrots add a necessary crunch and a pop of orange, though they take slightly longer to cook. For an adventurous twist, try spiralizing parsnips or daikon radish. These provide a peppery or earthy undertone that balances well with sweet BBQ glazes.

How to Prep and Assemble Your Skewers

The trick to making spiralized vegetable skewers is in the folding. You aren't just sliding a noodle onto a stick; you're creating a coil. Start by using your Vegetable Spiralizer to create long, continuous strands. If your noodles are too short, they'll slip off the skewer during the flip.

To assemble, hold the end of a vegetable ribbon against the skewer and gently wind it around the metal or wooden stick, overlapping the strands slightly. This creates a dense "spring" of vegetables. I recommend alternating colors—orange carrot, green zucchini, and yellow squash—to make the platter look professional. If you're using wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes first to prevent them from catching fire on the grill.

Flavor Pairings and Marinades

Because spiralized vegetables have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio than chunks, they absorb flavors incredibly fast. You don't need to marinate them for hours; 15 to 30 minutes is usually plenty. Avoid overly acidic marinades (like heavy vinegar) for too long, as the acid can break down the delicate structure of the spirals.

  • Lemon-Garlic Herb: Olive oil, fresh lemon juice, minced garlic, and chopped parsley. Great for a fresh, summer vibe.
  • Balsamic Glaze: A reduction of balsamic vinegar, honey, and a pinch of salt. This caramelizes beautifully over high heat.
  • Spicy Sriracha Lime: Sriracha, lime zest, and a touch of maple syrup for a sweet-and-heat kick.
  • Pesto Twist: Brush with a thin layer of basil pesto for an Italian-inspired side.

Grilling Tips for the Perfect Char

The goal is a charred exterior with a tender interior. Because these vegetable ribbons are thin, they cook much faster than a standard steak or corn cob. Use a medium-high heat setting. If the grill is too cold, the vegetables will steam rather than sear, and you'll lose that smoky BBQ flavor.

Place the skewers across the grates and sear for about 2-3 minutes per side. Use tongs to rotate them carefully so you don't unravel the spirals. You'll know they are done when the edges are slightly browned and the vegetables have softened but still retain a slight "snap." Brush on a final layer of glaze or melted butter during the last minute of grilling for a glossy, professional finish.

Serving and Storage

Spiralized vegetable skewers are best served immediately while the char is fresh. To make them a full meal, serve them alongside grilled halloumi cheese or shrimp. If you're prepping for a large party, you can assemble the skewers a few hours in advance and keep them refrigerated, but wait to apply the oil or marinade until right before they hit the grill to keep the vegetables crisp.

If you have leftovers, these actually make a great cold salad. Simply slide the vegetables off the skewers and toss them with a light vinaigrette. The charred flavor carries over well into a cold dish.

FAQ

Will the vegetables fall off the skewer?

As long as you wind the spirals tightly and overlap the strands, they should stay secure. Avoid overcooking them to the point of mushiness, as that is when they are most likely to slide off.

Can I use a handheld or countertop spiralizer for this?

Both work! A handheld Vegetable Spiralizer is great for quick, small batches, while a countertop model is more stable and efficient if you are making skewers for a large crowd.

What is the best oil to use for grilling spiralized veggies?

Use an oil with a high smoke point, such as avocado oil or grapeseed oil. This prevents the oil from burning and tasting bitter at the high temperatures required for a good sear.
